name: Rutherford's gold foil — the shell that bounced back
scope: The experiment that emptied the atom and found its heart. T1: Manchester, 1909 — Rutherford tells an undergraduate, Ernest Marsden, to check something nobody expected to find: whether any alpha particles come STRAIGHT BACK off a thin gold foil. Marsden sits in the dark counting faint scintillation flashes on a zinc-sulfide screen, and they are there — roughly 1 in 8,000 bounces back toward the source. T2: Rutherford's own account of the shock, from a Cambridge lecture on 15 October 1936: it was 'almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.' T3: the model it killed — J.J. Thomson's plum pudding, in which the positive charge was smeared thin through the whole atom; a smeared charge can never shove an alpha around, only a tiny concentrated one can. T4: Rutherford's 1911 conclusion — almost all the mass and all the positive charge sit in a nucleus about one hundred-thousandth the width of the atom; a grain of sand in the middle of a football field, everything else empty. T5: the honest caveat — Rutherford's own planetary atom was doomed the moment he drew it, because classical electrodynamics says an orbiting electron radiates and must spiral into the nucleus almost instantly; Niels Bohr, who came to Manchester in 1912, had to bolt quantum rules onto it in 1913 before atoms could stay standing. Further rungs: Geiger built his counter because counting flashes by eye in a blacked-out room was unbearable drudgery; the alpha source was radium; Rutherford's 1908 Nobel came in CHEMISTRY, which he joked was the fastest transformation he had ever measured; and in 1919 he fired alphas into nitrogen and knocked out protons — the first time a human being deliberately changed one element into another.
source: Grokipedia 'Ernest Rutherford' (consulted via browser; confirms 1909 gold foil with Geiger and Marsden, 1911 nuclear model, plum-pudding overturned, 1908 Nobel in Chemistry, 1919 nitrogen transmutation). Grokipedia 'Geiger-Marsden_experiments' attempted — article not found. Wikipedia 'Geiger-Marsden experiments' (Marsden an undergraduate; 1909 'On a Diffuse Reflection of the alpha-Particles'; ~1 in 8,000 backscattered; the 15-inch-shell quote dated to a Cambridge lecture 15 Oct 1936; 1911 paper 'The Scattering of alpha and beta Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom'). Wikipedia 'Rutherford model' (atom ~100,000x the nucleus's diameter; grain-of-sand-on-a-football-field comparison; Bohr's arrival and the quantum fix).
framing_note: The flagship DISCOVERY ladder for this sub-strand. T1 keys the ACT and the person — an undergraduate told to look for nothing, who found something — never the year. ACCURACY RAIL: Rutherford did not run the counting; Geiger and Marsden did, and the famous tissue-paper line was spoken in 1936, twenty-seven years after the fact, in a lecture — tell it as his later recollection, not as something he shouted at the bench. Do not state a foil thickness unless the build verifies one. Dinner-test payoff: T1 and T4 (the grain of sand in the football field — the kid can retell that the chair he is sitting on is almost entirely empty space). DISTRACTOR MINE: the plum pudding model itself, plus the other live-at-the-time atomic pictures (Nagaoka's Saturnian atom, the cubical atom, a solid indivisible Daltonian sphere) and real adjacent people (Geiger, Marsden, Thomson, Bohr, Soddy). Anti-restatement: never let the stem say 'the atom has a tiny dense nucleus' before asking what the deflections proved — describe the DARKROOM and the flashes and let the conclusion be recalled knowledge. T5 is the honest-caveat rung: the bank says out loud that the winning model was itself broken, and names who fixed it.

name: Thomson's corpuscles and Millikan's oil drops
scope: How the first subatomic particle was found and then weighed — and how the weighing went subtly wrong. T1: Cavendish Laboratory, 1897 — J.J. Thomson bends cathode rays with an electric field, something other experimenters had tried and failed to do, and finds the mass-to-charge ratio is over a thousand times smaller than a hydrogen ion's: a piece of matter far lighter than the lightest atom, at a moment when 'atom' meant 'the thing that cannot be cut'. T2: he refused to call it an electron for years — his word was 'corpuscles'. T3: 1904 — Thomson turns his corpuscles into a picture of the whole atom: negative specks studded through a sphere of positive charge, the plum pudding, the model Rutherford would blow apart five years later. T4: 1909-1913 — Robert Millikan and his graduate student Harvey Fletcher watch single oil droplets hang between charged plates and find the charge on them always comes in whole multiples of one indivisible lump; their figure, 1.592 x 10^-19 coulombs, is under one percent off today's value, and the small error traces to a wrong published number for the viscosity of air. T5: Feynman's 1974 Caltech commencement address, 'Cargo Cult Science' — after Millikan, published values for the electron's charge crept UPWARD year by year, because an experimenter who got a number far from Millikan's went hunting for a reason to throw it out, and one who got a number close to his did not. The measurement was corrected not by new apparatus but by people stopping deferring. Further rungs: Fletcher's papers, opened after his death, say Millikan made him give up sole authorship as a condition of his PhD; and Thomson's son George Paget Thomson won the 1937 Nobel for showing the electron diffracts like a wave — the father proved it was a particle, the son proved it was a wave, and both were right.
source: Wikipedia 'J. J. Thomson' (May-June 1897 Crookes tube; electric deflection others had failed at; mass-to-charge over a thousand times lower than H+; 'corpuscles'; 1904 plum pudding; 1906 Nobel; G. P. Thomson's 1937 Nobel for electron diffraction). Wikipedia 'Oil drop experiment' (Millikan and Fletcher 1909-1913; result 1.5924(17) x 10^-19 C vs modern 1.602176634 x 10^-19 C; the wrong air-viscosity value as the error source; Gerald Holton's 1978 notebook analysis and Goodstein's reply; Feynman's 1974 'Cargo Cult Science' account of the creeping values; the Fletcher authorship dispute from papers released after his death).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY ladder with a MECHANISM spine and a self-deception payoff. T1 inverts the wonder: put the astonishing thing in the stem (something lighter than the lightest atom, in 1897, when atoms were by definition uncuttable) and make the knowable thing the answer. ACCURACY RAIL: the data-selection charge against Millikan is contested and must be told honestly — Holton found more measurements in the notebooks than in the paper; Millikan's own 1913 paper says he used only drops with a complete series of observations, and Goodstein's later reading of the notebooks supports him. The bank does NOT convict Millikan of fraud. The SOLID, undisputed fact is Feynman's: the published values crept up afterwards because later experimenters deferred to his number. Key T5 to that, not to an accusation. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (why grown-up scientists kept getting the same answer slightly wrong for years) and T1. DISTRACTOR MINE: real rival ideas of what cathode rays were (waves in the ether, charged molecules of the residual gas, 'radiant matter'), and real adjacent people (Crookes, Lenard, Hertz, Millikan, Fletcher, Perrin). Teach 'ion' and 'charge quantisation' before testing them.
history_overlap: HOW-SCIENCE section (same bank): if a self-deception / replication ladder is built there, Feynman's 1974 'Cargo Cult Science' lecture is the shared source. This ladder keys it ONLY to the electron-charge values creeping up after Millikan; leave the replication crisis, p-hacking and Ioannidis 2005 to that ladder.

name: Becquerel's drawer — radioactivity found by a week of clouds
scope: The accident that only counts as an accident if you develop the failed plate. T1: Paris, late February 1896 — Henri Becquerel wraps a photographic plate in thick black paper, lays uranium salt crystals and a metal shape on top, and waits for sunshine to make the crystals phosphoresce. The sun stays behind cloud for days, so he shoves the whole package into a dark drawer. On 1 March he develops the plate anyway, and the silhouettes are there, blazing. T2: his hypothesis was WRONG, and that is the point — he believed sunlight had to charge the crystals up first. The drawer proved the uranium needed nothing at all: no light, no heat, no chemistry, and it never stopped. T3: the crisis this created in 1896 physics — a lump of uranium sitting in a closed drawer pours out energy indefinitely with no fuel and no visible change, which looked like conservation of energy simply failing. T4: Marie Curie's decisive contribution to the puzzle — she measured, with Pierre's electrometer, that the emission is proportional to the amount of uranium present and is untouched by heating it, dissolving it or combining it into compounds. That meant it was a property of the ATOM, not of the substance, which is the first crack in the idea of the atom as an unchanging thing. T5: 1901 — Becquerel carried a small tube of radium in his waistcoat pocket for a few hours; weeks later the skin over that pocket ulcerated, and the burn took months to heal. He published the observation, and that report is where radiotherapy starts. He shared the 1903 Nobel in Physics with the Curies.
source: Wikipedia 'Henri Becquerel' (the sunlight/phosphorescence hypothesis; plates wrapped in black paper with a coin; the overcast days and the drawer on 26-27 February 1896; plates developed 1 March 1896, silhouettes 'appeared with great intensity'; by May 1896 he concluded uranium emits spontaneously; the 1901 waistcoat-pocket radium burn that led to radiotherapy; the 1903 Nobel shared with the Curies). Wikipedia 'Marie Curie' (the Curies' coinage of 'radioactivity'; her electrometer measurements).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY + REVERSAL ladder built on a wrong hypothesis that survived contact with a result. T1 must be SCENE-LED: the black paper, the clouds, the drawer, the plate he had every reason to bin. ACCURACY RAIL: this is routinely mis-told as pure luck. It was not — Becquerel already had uranium salts to hand because his family had studied phosphorescence in that same Paris laboratory for two generations before him, and he developed the plate precisely because he was a careful man checking a null result. THE BUILD MUST VERIFY the Becquerel-dynasty detail (three generations holding the same physics chair at the Museum national d'Histoire naturelle) before any rung asserts it. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a cloudy week discovered radioactivity because one man developed a picture that should have been blank). DISTRACTOR MINE: the live wrong ideas of 1896 — X-rays, phosphorescence, ordinary fluorescence, ether disturbances, plate contamination — plus real adjacent people (Rontgen, Poincare, the Curies, Rutherford). Anti-restatement: never let the stem say 'uranium emits radiation on its own' before asking what the drawer showed. Lane note: the medical use of radium belongs to the life/medicine strand; here the burn rung is an OBSERVATION Becquerel made on his own body, which is the test-it-yourself thread.

name: The Curies' shed — tonnes of ore for a tenth of a gram
scope: Four years of physical labour to prove a number. T1: the puzzle that started it — Marie measured pitchblende ore and found it more radioactive than its uranium content could possibly explain. The ore was hotter than pure uranium. Rather than assume a bad measurement, she concluded something unknown was hiding in it, and went to find it. T2: the workplace — a leaky, unheated former dissecting shed off the rue Lhomond, no ventilation, where she stirred boiling cauldrons of ore with an iron rod nearly as tall as she was; the chemist Wilhelm Ostwald, visiting, described it as a cross between a stable and a potato cellar. T3: the yield — tonnes of pitchblende residue worked down over about four years to roughly one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride by 1902. Polonium was announced in July 1898 and named for her occupied homeland; radium on 26 December 1898; and the Curies coined the word 'radioactivity' itself. T4: the glow — in her 1923 memoir of Pierre she wrote of going into the workroom at night to see the faintly luminous silhouettes on every shelf: 'the glowing tubes looked like faint, fairy lights.' They kept a tube by the bed. They did not know it was killing them. T5: the 1903 Nobel in Physics — a committee member privately warned Pierre that only he and Becquerel had been nominated; Pierre objected, and Marie's name was added. In 1911 she took the Chemistry Nobel alone, and remains the only person with Nobels in two different sciences. T6: 1914-18 — she built about twenty mobile radiography vans, the 'petites Curies', learned to drive, and got X-ray units to the front. T7: the payoff — her notebooks are STILL too radioactive to hand out. They sit in lead-lined boxes at the Bibliotheque nationale, and a reader must wear protective clothing and sign a liability waiver. The contaminant is radium-226, half-life about 1,600 years, so a century has barely dented it. T8: she died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia.
source: Grokipedia 'Marie Sklodowska-Curie' (consulted via browser; 1903 Physics and 1911 Chemistry Nobels, the only person with Nobels in two sciences, petites Curies, death from aplastic anaemia 4 July 1934, the Flying University, Pierre's death 1906). Wikipedia 'Marie Curie' (polonium announced July 1898, radium 26 December 1898, 'radioactivity' coined by the Curies; the converted shed next to ESPCI, a former dissecting room, poorly ventilated and not waterproof; one tonne of pitchblende to one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride in 1902; the 1903 nomination complaint by Pierre; the papers too dangerous to handle, kept in lead-lined boxes; the petites Curies and over a million wounded examined). Marie Curie, 'Pierre Curie' (1923) for the 'faint, fairy lights' passage, corroborated via quotation collections. Reporting on the Bibliotheque nationale holdings (protective clothing and a signed liability waiver; radium-226 half-life ~1,600 years).
framing_note: Flagship DISCOVERY ladder; the wonder is the LABOUR, not the glamour. T1 keys the ladder to a MEASUREMENT she refused to explain away — that is the scientific virtue the rung is teaching. ACCURACY RAIL: do not state a precise tonnage as settled. Sources vary between roughly one tonne of ore and several tonnes of residue processed over four years; the safe, checkable statement is 'tonnes of pitchblende residue worked down to about a tenth of a gram of radium chloride by 1902'. Also: the 'fairy lights' line is a real published quote from her 1923 memoir of Pierre and must be attributed to that book; the Ostwald 'stable and potato cellar' description must be verified in the build before use. Dinner-test payoff: T7 (her notebooks are still radioactive and you have to sign a waiver to read them). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent scientists and elements — Becquerel, Debierne, Rutherford, Soddy, actinium, thorium, uranium, polonium — and the live wrong ideas about what radium's energy came from (a chemical reaction, absorbed ether energy, phosphorescence). Anti-restatement: describe the anomaly (the ore is hotter than its uranium) and let 'a new element' be recalled, never stated in the stem.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank may carry Marie Curie as a women's-history or WWI figure, in which case the 'petites Curies' X-ray vans are the likeliest shared fact. If so, drop that rung here or re-key it to the physics (she trained the operators and ran the tubes off a car engine's dynamo). Science keeps the measurement, the isolation and the contaminated notebooks.

name: Chadwick's neutron — the particle two great labs walked past
scope: A REVERSAL about naming what you see wrongly. T1: Cambridge, February 1932 — James Chadwick fires the mysterious 'beryllium radiation' at a slab of paraffin wax and watches protons come flying out of it, hard. In about a fortnight of near-continuous work he shows the only thing that can knock a proton that hard is something with a proton's own mass and no electric charge at all. T2: the miss — Bothe and Becker in Berlin had produced the radiation in 1930 and called it gamma rays. In Paris in January 1932, Irene and Frederic Joliot-Curie ran the paraffin experiment FIRST and also called it gamma rays, which would have required gammas of about 50 MeV, an absurd energy. Two Nobel-calibre laboratories had the neutron passing through their apparatus and gave it the wrong name. T3: how Chadwick actually proved it — he changed the target, from hydrogen to nitrogen, measured the recoil speeds, and applied conservation of momentum; only one value of the unknown particle's mass fits both results at once. That is the whole trick, and a fifteen-year-old can follow it. T4: it was not a bolt from the blue. Rutherford had CONJECTURED a neutral particle of roughly proton mass in his 1920 Bakerian Lecture, and Chadwick had been hunting it on and off for twelve years. T5: why it changed everything within seven years — a neutral particle is not pushed away by the nucleus's positive charge, so it can walk straight in; that is what makes fission possible, and it is why uranium can be split with slow neutrons and not with protons. Chadwick took the 1935 Nobel. Further rungs: Chadwick spent the whole of the First World War interned as an enemy alien at Ruhleben camp near Berlin, where he ran physics lectures for fellow prisoners; and he ended up in physics at all because he joined the wrong queue at Manchester registration and stayed after hearing Rutherford's first lecture; and his own 1914 measurement — that beta-decay electrons emerge with a continuous SPREAD of energies — is the anomaly that would force Pauli to invent the neutrino.
source: Grokipedia 'James Chadwick' (consulted via browser; neutron 1932 at the Cavendish under Rutherford; 1935 Nobel; the 1914 continuous beta spectrum result in Berlin under Geiger; internment at Ruhleben from November 1914 and the camp science lectures; the accidental physics enrolment queue at Manchester in 1908). Wikipedia 'Discovery of the neutron' (Bothe and Becker 1930 beryllium radiation; the Joliot-Curies' 1932 paraffin experiment and their gamma-ray misinterpretation requiring an impossible ~50 MeV; Chadwick's 'Possible Existence of a Neutron' letter to Nature, 1932; conservation of momentum with different target nuclei to fix the mass; Rutherford's 1920 Bakerian Lecture conjecture of a neutral particle).
framing_note: A REVERSAL/DISCOVERY ladder whose lesson is that seeing a thing and correctly naming it are different acts. T1 keys the ACT (paraffin, recoiling protons, a fortnight) not the date. ACCURACY RAIL: sources differ on whether the Nature letter appeared in February or March 1932 — the build must pin it against the Nature record before writing any rung on the date, and should key every rung to the measurement rather than to a calendar. Also do not caricature the Joliot-Curies: they were superb experimentalists who went on to a Nobel of their own; the honest telling is that a wrong prior about what the radiation MUST be filtered out what it was. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (two of the best labs in the world had the answer in their hands and named it wrong). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real rival interpretations of the beryllium radiation (high-energy gamma rays, Compton recoil, a proton-electron composite) and real adjacent people (Bothe, Becker, the Joliot-Curies, Rutherford, Geiger). Teach 'conservation of momentum' as a working tool in T3 before testing it. LANE: Chadwick led the British Mission to the Manhattan Project — that is history's, and no rung here goes near it.

name: Meitner's Christmas walk — fission worked out in exile
scope: The physics done by the person who was not allowed to be in the room. T1: Kungalv, Sweden, Christmas 1938 — Lise Meitner, a refugee with no laboratory and no proper job, is out in the snow with her nephew Otto Frisch when she does the arithmetic on a scrap of paper: the two fragments weigh LESS than the uranium nucleus they came from, and by E=mc-squared the missing mass is worth about 200 million electron-volts of energy for every single atom that splits. T2: the letter that set it off — Otto Hahn wrote to her on 19 December 1938 to say that he and Fritz Strassmann had found BARIUM in neutron-bombarded uranium, an element barely half uranium's weight, that he could not explain it, and that he needed her physics. T3: the mechanism — Bohr's liquid-drop nucleus. The captured neutron makes the drop wobble; once it stretches far enough, the electric repulsion between the two ends beats the surface tension holding it together, and the drop pinches in two. T4: the word — back in Copenhagen, Frisch asked a colleague at Bohr's institute what biologists call a cell splitting in two, was told 'binary fission', and that is where 'nuclear fission' comes from. Frisch then confirmed the split experimentally within days by catching the fragments' enormous energy pulse. T5: the snub — the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Otto Hahn alone. Meitner had been on the problem for thirty years, had left Berlin in July 1938 only because she was Jewish, and had supplied the explanation Hahn could not produce; the Nobel archives, opened decades later, show a committee that treated the whole thing as chemistry and never seriously weighed the physics. T6: she was invited to work on the bomb and refused. She loathed the newspapers' label for her, 'the Jewish mother of the bomb'. T7: element 109 was named meitnerium in 1997. T8: her escape — 13 July 1938, out of Berlin by train with no exit visa, met at the Dutch border by Dirk Coster; Hahn had given her a diamond ring to sell if she needed money.
source: Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (consulted via browser; the December 1938 interpretation of Hahn and Strassmann's barium result; the liquid-drop deformation, ~200 MeV per fission, the coining of 'fission' with Frisch; Hahn's letter of 19 December 1938; the Kungalv Christmas meeting with Frisch; the 1944 Chemistry Nobel to Hahn alone and the archival account of her exclusion; the 13 July 1938 escape with Dirk Coster and Hahn's diamond ring; element 109 named meitnerium in 1997; her ethical reservations about weapons). Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission' (Frisch's naming after a discussion with William A. Arnold, who suggested 'binary fission'; ~200 MeV per event; Meitner-Frisch letter in Nature). Wikipedia 'Otto Robert Frisch' (the Christmas 1938 Kungalv visit; his January 1939 Copenhagen confirmation; the Nature paper).
framing_note: Flagship DISCOVERY ladder plus the sub-strand's one genuine institutional-failure rung — hence vision_mandated. ACTIVE VOICE IS LOAD-BEARING: a person did each of these things and the rung names them. Do not write 'the prize was awarded to Hahn'; write who decided. ACCURACY RAILS, three of them: (1) the Meitner-Frisch letter to Nature was written on 16 January 1939 and published on 11 February 1939, and Frisch's separate experimental letter was written 17 January — do not conflate them or write a rung on a single 'fission paper' date. (2) The 1944 Chemistry prize was announced in November 1945; say it right. (3) Do NOT cite a count of Nobel nominations unless the build checks the Nobel nomination archive. Also: William Arnold's discipline is described differently across sources — the checkable fact is that Frisch borrowed the word from BIOLOGY, so key the rung to the borrowing, not to Arnold's job title. FAIRNESS RAIL: Hahn is not a villain. He did credit her privately, he was working under a regime that forbade publishing a Jewish collaborator's name, and the failure the rung names is the committee's. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the physics of the atomic age was worked out on a walk in the snow by a woman who had just lost her country) and T5. DISTRACTOR MINE: real rival explanations live in 1938 — transuranic elements, radium-like products, alpha chains — plus real adjacent people (Hahn, Strassmann, Frisch, Bohr, Fermi, Joliot-Curie, Noddack). Ida Noddack, who suggested in 1934 that uranium might break into large fragments and was ignored, is a superb T4 rung and a superb distractor.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank owns the Manhattan Project and the Second World War as narrative. This ladder never tells the bomb story; the only bomb-adjacent rung is Meitner's REFUSAL to work on it, which is her act, not the war. If history carries a 'scientists who fled Hitler' ladder, her 13 July 1938 escape is the shared fact — keep the science rung keyed to the physics she did once she got out.

name: Half-life and the radiometric clocks
scope: CONCEPT/THEME ladder — one idea deepened across the named cases that display it. T1: the rule that makes clocks possible — a lump of radioactive material always loses half its atoms in the same stretch of time, whatever the size of the lump; and nothing you can do to it (heat it, freeze it, crush it, dissolve it, burn it into a compound) changes that stretch. That immunity to everything is exactly what makes it a clock, and it is why no other timekeeper works on a rock. T2: the strangeness underneath — you cannot say WHEN any single atom will go. Each one has the same chance every second and never ages; an atom that has sat there for a billion years is no closer to decaying than one made this morning. The clock is trustworthy only because there are trillions of atoms in the sample. T3: Willard Libby's test of his own method at Chicago, 1949 — he dated wood from Egyptian tombs whose ages were already known from written records: independently dated to 2625 BC, radiocarbon said about 2800 BC. He is the rare case of a man who published the check before the claim, and took the 1960 Chemistry Nobel. T4: the REVERSAL — raw radiocarbon dates turned out to be systematically WRONG, because the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has never been constant. The fix came from counting the growth rings of bristlecone pines, one year at a time, to build a calibration curve. A nuclear clock had to be corrected by a tree. T5: reading a body — the Iceman found in the Otztal Alps on 19 September 1991 was radiocarbon-dated to between 3359 and 3105 BC, and it took until a 2001 CT scan for anyone to notice the arrowhead in his left shoulder. T6: the biggest number the method has produced — Clair Patterson, 1953-56, measured lead isotopes in fragments of the Canyon Diablo meteorite and got 4.55 billion years for the age of the Earth, replacing a best estimate of 3.3 billion; that figure has stood essentially unchanged for seventy years. T7: what it cost him to get it — lead contamination was everywhere in his laboratory, in his chemicals, his air and his own hair, so he had to build one of the first clean rooms at Caltech before the measurement would even hold still. T8: the bomb pulse — above-ground nuclear tests between 1950 and 1963 nearly doubled the carbon-14 in the atmosphere, peaking in 1964, and the falling tail is now itself a clock for anything that has been alive since.
source: Wikipedia 'Half-life' (Rutherford's 1907 'half-life period', shortened in the early 1950s; the statistical nature — 50% probability per half-life, no prediction for an individual atom; Rutherford's application to dating rocks). Wikipedia 'Radiocarbon dating' (Libby at Chicago from 1945, the Egyptian tomb check — 2625 BC +/- 75 known vs ~2800 BC +/- 250 measured; 1960 Nobel; Libby vs modern half-life values 5568 and 5730 years; the dendrochronology/bristlecone calibration correcting systematic error; the 1950-1963 bomb pulse peaking in 1964; the ~50,000-year limit; AMS). Wikipedia 'Otzi' (found 19 September 1991 by Helmut and Erika Simon; dated 3359-3105 BC; arrowhead found by CT scan in 2001). Wikipedia 'Clair Cameron Patterson' (4.55 billion years from Canyon Diablo meteorite lead isotopes, published 1956, previously accepted 3.3 billion; the Caltech clean room in 1953; lead contamination in his own hair).
framing_note: THE ANALYTIC BACKBONE of this sub-strand — a theme ladder with a native T4/T5 ceiling, deepening ONE method across named cases. Teach 'half-life' and 'isotope' explicitly before testing either. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) the 'nothing changes a half-life' claim needs its honest exception at T5 — electron-capture decay rates do shift very slightly with chemical environment (beryllium-7 is the standard example), by well under one percent; the build must verify the size of the effect before writing that rung, and must present it as a real measured exception, not as a loophole that undermines dating. (2) Radiocarbon uses two half-life values by convention (the 5568-year 'Libby half-life' for reported ages, 5730 as the better measurement) — do not write a rung asserting a single number without saying which. (3) Do not let a rung imply radiocarbon dates rocks; it dates once-living carbon, out to about 50,000 years. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a nuclear clock corrected by counting tree rings) and T2 (an atom does not age). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real superseded methods and wrong answers — Kelvin's cooling-Earth estimate of tens of millions of years, Halley's ocean-salt clock, Joly's estimates, counting sediment layers, and the pre-Patterson 3.3-billion figure — plus real adjacent people (Rutherford, Soddy, Boltwood, Libby, Patterson, Holmes). Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'atmospheric carbon-14 has varied' before asking what the tree rings fixed.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank may own the Shroud of Turin dating controversy — leave it out here entirely. If the Iceman appears in another bank (history or animal), this ladder owns ONLY the dating — the radiocarbon range and the calibration that makes such a range trustworthy — never his life, kit, tattoos or killing. GEOGRAPHY tours places; the Otztal Alps are scenery here, not subject.

name: The cloud chamber — how to see a single particle
scope: The TEST-IT-YOURSELF flagship: the one apparatus in this whole sub-strand a kid can build. T1: 1894 — C. T. R. Wilson takes a temporary relief post at the observatory on the summit of Ben Nevis and spends a fortnight watching sunlight throw his own shadow onto cloud, ringed with colour. He goes back to Cambridge determined to make clouds indoors, in a jar, and spends the next seventeen years on it. T2: the accident — to make a cloud you normally need dust for droplets to grow on. Wilson found that in scrupulously dust-free air a cloud still formed if he expanded it hard enough, because IONS work as seeds too. A meteorologist chasing weather had built a detector for the invisible. T3: how the trick works — a charged particle rips electrons off the molecules it passes, leaving a line of ions; supersaturated vapour condenses on that line; and you see a thread of fog exactly where the particle went, seconds after it has gone. Wilson shared the 1927 Nobel with Arthur Compton. T4: what people saw in the fog — on 2 August 1932 Carl Anderson photographed a track curving the WRONG way in a magnetic field. He had put a lead plate across the middle of his chamber so the particle would lose speed crossing it, which told him which direction it was travelling, which told him the charge was positive and the mass was an electron's. Dirac's predicted anti-electron, photographed. Anderson had the Nobel at 31. T5: the fog kept delivering — Anderson found the muon in 1936, and Rochester and Butler found the kaon in 1947; for roughly forty years the fastest route to a new particle was to sit and stare at condensation. T6: BUILD ONE — a sealed clear box, felt soaked in isopropyl alcohol along the warm top, dry ice under a black metal floor, a dark room and a bright light from the side. Within a minute you are watching cosmic-ray muons and the decay products of radon crossing your kitchen. They were always crossing it.
source: Wikipedia 'Cloud chamber' (Wilson inspired by the Brocken spectre on Ben Nevis in 1894; expansion chamber perfected 1911; half the 1927 Nobel, shared with Arthur Compton; ions as condensation nuclei; Blackett's spring-driven pulsed chambers; Langsdorf's 1936 diffusion chamber; positron 1932, muon 1936, kaon 1947 by Rochester and Butler; home diffusion-chamber construction with isopropanol vapour, a warm top plate, a cold bottom plate and dry ice). Wikipedia 'Positron' (Dirac's 1928 equation and his initial identification of the negative-energy solution with the proton, then the 1931 anti-electron prediction; Anderson's photograph of 2 August 1932; the lead plate used to establish direction of travel; the name 'positron' suggested by the Physical Review editor, not by Anderson; 1936 Nobel; Chung-Yao Chao's unexplored 1929 anomalies).
framing_note: The TEST-IT-YOURSELF soul of the sub-strand, and the ladder that most deserves an invitation framing: the final rung is a build, not a fact. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) Wilson was chasing METEOROLOGY, not particles — the detector was a by-product of trying to understand cloud formation, and the ladder must not retro-fit him with the intention. (2) Anderson did NOT coin 'positron'; the Physical Review editor suggested it. (3) Do not say the chamber shows you the particle — it shows you a trail of condensation left behind it, which is a different and more interesting claim, and T3 must make that distinction the wonder. Dinner-test payoff: T6 (there are particles going through you right now and here is the shopping list to see them) and T4 (the lead plate — a slab of metal is how you tell which way a thing was going). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent detectors and their inventors (Geiger counter, bubble chamber and Glaser, photographic emulsion, spark chamber, scintillation screen) and real adjacent particles that were found or mis-called in fog (the muon initially mistaken for Yukawa's predicted meson is a superb T5 rung and a superb distractor). SAFETY: the build rung must name dry-ice handling (gloves, ventilation) plainly and briefly, without turning the invitation into a warning label.

name: Pauli's ghost — the particle invented to save a law
scope: A MYSTERY-to-MECHANISM ladder about proposing something you cannot see. T1: 4 December 1930 — Wolfgang Pauli will not travel to a physics meeting in Tubingen, so he sends a letter instead, addressed 'Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen', proposing what he himself calls a 'desperate remedy': an invisible, chargeless, nearly massless particle that sneaks off with the energy nobody can account for. T2: the crime he was solving — James Chadwick had shown in 1914 that the electrons coming out of beta decay emerge with a SPREAD of energies, from almost nothing up to a sharp maximum, where every other kind of decay gives one clean value. Energy was apparently going missing, and Niels Bohr was prepared to abandon conservation of energy inside the nucleus rather than invent a new particle. Pauli chose the particle. T3: the name — Pauli called his particle a 'neutron'. When Chadwick's real neutron took that word in 1932, Fermi's group in Rome renamed Pauli's the 'neutrino', the little neutral one, on Edoardo Amaldi's joke. T4: the twenty-six-year hunt — Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan first proposed catching neutrinos in the fireball of a 20-kiloton nuclear test, with a detector nicknamed El Monstro dropped down a shaft forty metres from ground zero; a colleague talked them into a nuclear reactor instead. They called it Project Poltergeist. T5: the trick that made it work — Savannah River, 1956, twelve metres underground. An antineutrino hits a proton and makes a positron and a neutron. The positron annihilates instantly, giving two gamma flashes; the neutron blunders about for a few microseconds and is then swallowed by dissolved cadmium, giving another. Two flashes, microseconds apart, in that order, is a signature nothing else fakes. T6: the scale — about 65 billion neutrinos from the Sun cross every square centimetre of you every second, day and night, straight through the Earth at night, and in an entire human lifetime perhaps one of them will stop inside you. T7: the anomaly that looked like a disaster — Ray Davis's tank of dry-cleaning fluid in the Homestake gold mine counted only about a third of the solar neutrinos the Sun should be sending. For thirty years most people assumed the model of the Sun was wrong. It was not: the neutrinos were changing type on the way over. Kajita and McDonald took the 2015 Nobel for proving it. T8: STILL OPEN, and the bank says so — nobody knows how much a neutrino actually weighs (only that the three kinds together come to under about 0.06 electron-volts), and nobody knows whether a neutrino is its own antiparticle.
source: Grokipedia 'Neutrino' (consulted via browser; Pauli's 1930 prediction and the 1956 Cowan-Reines detection; three flavours; trillions through the body every second; oscillation and the PMNS matrix; the solar neutrino problem and its resolution; sum of masses under 0.064 eV at 95% CL as of 2025; the open Dirac-vs-Majorana question; ~99% of a core-collapse supernova's energy carried off by neutrinos). Wikipedia 'Neutrino' (Amaldi's coinage of 'neutrino'; Cowan-Reines published in Science, 20 July 1956; ~6.5 x 10^10 solar neutrinos per square centimetre per second; Homestake deficit; 2015 Nobel to Kajita and McDonald). Wikipedia 'Cowan-Reines neutrino experiment' (the 1951 plan to use a 20-kiloton test with the 'El Monstro' detector in a shaft 40 m from the detonation, authorised by Norris Bradbury; J. M. B. Kellogg's redirection to a reactor; Hanford 1953 then Savannah River from late 1955, 12 m underground; 'Project Poltergeist'; the inverse-beta delayed-coincidence signature with cadmium). Wikipedia 'Clyde Cowan' (Reines's 1995 Nobel alone, Cowan having died in 1974). CERN timeline and ETH Zurich Pauli exhibition pages on the 4 December 1930 'Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen' letter and the 'desperate remedy' phrase.
framing_note: A MYSTERY ladder that resolves into MECHANISM and then honestly re-opens. CRITICAL ACCURACY RAIL: the famous line 'I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected' is NOT documented in Pauli's letter and must never appear in this bank — the bank bans unsourced quotes. The verified phrase is 'desperate remedy', from the 4 December 1930 letter, and the salutation 'Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen'. Second rail: the 1956 telegram to Pauli and his reported reply are widely retold but the build MUST verify the wording before any rung uses it; if it cannot, key the rung to the detection instead. Third rail: 65 billion solar neutrinos per square centimetre per SECOND — several popular sources garble this to 'per year'. Dinner-test payoff: T6 (they are going through you and through the whole Earth right now) and T1 (he skipped the conference for a ball and posted the idea instead). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real live alternative — Bohr's serious proposal to give up energy conservation inside the nucleus — plus real adjacent particles and people (Chadwick's neutron, Fermi, Amaldi, Davis, Bahcall, Reines, Cowan). T8 is a genuine MYSTERY rung: say 'no one yet knows' proudly, and make sure no distractor secretly states the truth.

name: E=mc-squared in the Sun — where sunlight actually comes from
scope: The mass-deficit made personal. T1: four hydrogen nuclei go in and one helium nucleus comes out, and the helium weighs about 0.7 percent LESS than the four did. That missing 0.7 percent is the warmth on the back of your hand. T2: the scale — the Sun fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second and turns about 4 million tonnes of that straight into energy, every second, and has been doing so for 4.6 billion years while getting through only about half its fuel. T3: the problem that forced the answer — Lord Kelvin, using the best physics of his day (a Sun heated by its own gravitational contraction), calculated the Sun could only be tens of millions of years old, and used the number to attack geologists and Darwin, who needed vastly longer. Kelvin's arithmetic was sound and his answer was wrong, because nuclear energy did not yet exist in anybody's equations; Arthur Eddington said as much out loud in 1920, before anyone could prove it. T4: the bottleneck — the very first step, two protons sticking together to make deuterium, requires one of them to turn into a neutron by the weak force at the same instant, and that is so improbable that the average proton in the Sun's core waits about NINE BILLION YEARS for its turn. The Sun is slow, and that is precisely why it is still here. T5: two protons should never touch at all. Even at 15.7 million degrees they do not have enough energy to beat their own electrical repulsion; they get through the barrier by quantum tunnelling — the same idea George Gamow used in 1928 to explain alpha decay, run backwards. T6: light made in the core takes somewhere between about ten thousand and a hundred and seventy thousand years to random-walk its way out to the surface, while the neutrinos made in the very same reactions are out in 2.3 seconds. The sunlight on your face is ancient; the neutrinos arriving with it are eight minutes old. T7: Hans Bethe worked out the reaction networks in stars in 1938-39 and collected the physics Nobel for it in 1967. T8: how we CHECK a place we can never visit — neutrino detectors look straight into the core in real time, which is the only direct measurement of the Sun's interior anyone has ever made.
source: Wikipedia 'Proton-proton chain' (the four branches; ~0.7% of the protons' mass converted; 26.73 MeV per completed chain; the first step initiated by the weak nuclear force and requiring quantum tunnelling; 'the average proton in the core of the Sun waits 9 billion years before it successfully fuses'; core ~15.5 million K; Eddington's 1920s proposal; Bethe's 1939 work and 1967 Nobel). Wikipedia 'Sun' (about 600 billion kg of hydrogen fused per second; about 4 billion kg of matter converted to energy per second; core close to 15.7 million K and up to 150 g per cubic centimetre; photon travel time from core to surface estimated between 10,000 and 170,000 years; neutrinos take 2.3 seconds to reach the surface).
framing_note: A MECHANISM ladder with a REVERSAL rung. T1 INVERTS THE WONDER properly: put the arithmetic in the stem (four in, one out, 0.7 percent missing) and make the physical consequence the answer. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) do not give Kelvin a single number — he published estimates ranging over tens to hundreds of millions of years and narrowed them over his career; the rung's content is the SHAPE of the error (right method, missing physics), not a figure. (2) Eddington's 1920 British Association address is the documented moment he argued for subatomic energy in stars; the build must verify any quoted wording before using it. (3) Photon escape time is a wide range in the literature (roughly ten thousand to a few hundred thousand years) — give it as a range and say why it is a range (a random walk, not a straight line), never as a single number. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a proton waits nine billion years for its turn) and T6 (the light is old, the neutrinos are eight minutes old). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real superseded theories of solar energy — gravitational contraction (Kelvin-Helmholtz), ordinary chemical burning, meteor infall, radioactive decay of a solar core — all of them held by serious people, plus real adjacent scientists (Kelvin, Helmholtz, Eddington, Bethe, Gamow, Payne-Gaposchkin). Teach 'fusion' and 'mass deficit' before testing them.
history_overlap: EARTH/SPACE section (same bank): a 'life cycle of stars' or 'made of star stuff / nucleosynthesis' ladder would own supernovae, element-forging and the H-R diagram — this ladder owns only the proton-proton chain's nuclear arithmetic and how it is checked. Also internal: the solar-neutrino deficit and its resolution belong to the NEUTRINO ladder in this same sub-strand; here the neutrino rung is keyed to 'we can watch the core in real time', not to oscillation.

name: The Higgs — a forty-eight-year wait for one particle
scope: What it looks like to predict something and then live long enough to be checked. T1: in 1964 Peter Higgs wrote a short paper and the journal Physics Letters, edited at CERN, turned it down as of no obvious relevance to physics. He added one extra paragraph — pointing out that his idea implied a brand-new massive particle nobody had ever seen — and sent it to Physical Review Letters, which printed it. That single added paragraph is why the particle carries his name and not somebody else's. T2: three groups got there independently within months of each other in 1964 — Francois Englert and Robert Brout in Brussels in August, Higgs in Edinburgh in October, and Gerald Guralnik, Carl Hagen and Tom Kibble in November. Six people, one mechanism, one name on it. T3: what the field does — particles that interact strongly with the Higgs field behave heavy; photons do not interact with it at all and stay massless, which is why light is fast and you are not. T4: the correction that has to be said out loud — the Higgs field does NOT give you most of your weight. About 99 percent of the mass of a proton is the binding energy of the quarks and gluons churning inside it, not the Higgs. T5: 4 July 2012, CERN — ATLAS and CMS, two collaborations deliberately kept independent so that each could check the other, announced the same bump at about 125 GeV. Higgs, aged 83, sat in the seminar room and said it was incredible it had happened in his lifetime. Forty-eight years. T6: the nickname he hated — 'the God particle' comes from the title of Leon Lederman's 1993 book, a title his publisher pushed; Higgs, an atheist, objected that it muddled people about what the science claimed. T7: the question the discovery OPENED — the boson's measured mass, 125.11 GeV, is far lighter than a naive quantum calculation says it should be, the hierarchy problem, and nobody knows why. Say so.
source: Grokipedia 'Higgs boson' (consulted via browser; 1964 prediction by Englert and Brout, Higgs, and Guralnik, Hagen and Kibble independently; discovery 4 July 2012 by ATLAS and CMS at the LHC; Englert and Higgs share the 2013 Nobel; spin-zero, no charge; mass ~125 GeV, over 130 times a proton's, lifetime ~10^-22 s; refined mass 125.11 +/- 0.11 GeV from ATLAS; the hierarchy problem stated as open). Wikipedia 'Higgs boson' (the three 1964 PRL papers with months; ~99% of proton and neutron mass from QCD binding energy rather than the Higgs field; Lederman's 1993 book as the source of 'God particle'; Brout's death in 2011 making him ineligible in 2013). Wikipedia 'Peter Higgs' (the Physics Letters rejection as 'of no obvious relevance to physics'; the added paragraph predicting a massive spin-zero boson; publication in Physical Review Letters; his remark at the 2012 Geneva seminar; his objection to 'God particle'; his death on 8 April 2024).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY ladder whose wonder is PATIENCE and whose T4 is a corrected-misconception rung, which is on-voice gold. T1 keys the ACT (a rejected paper, one added paragraph) and not the year. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) the theory is properly the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism and six people published it in 1964 — a rung that says 'Higgs predicted it' alone is wrong, and T2 exists to fix that. (2) Do not write that the Higgs field is what makes things heavy: about 99 percent of ordinary matter's mass is QCD binding energy, and T4 is the rung that says so. (3) Mass figures: quote 125.11 +/- 0.11 GeV or 'about 125 GeV', never a bare 126. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the paper was rejected, and the paragraph he added to answer the rejection is the whole reason it's called the Higgs boson) and T5 (he was 83). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent particles and concepts that the kid can plausibly confuse — W and Z bosons, gluons, the top quark, the photon, supersymmetric partners — plus the real co-discoverers as name distractors (Englert, Brout, Kibble, Guralnik, Hagen, Nambu, Anderson). GRADE-10 CEILING: no gauge theory, no spontaneous symmetry breaking in formal terms. Describe the field as something particles interact with, more or less strongly, and stop there. T7 is a MYSTERY rung — no distractor may secretly be the answer to the hierarchy problem.

name: Oklo — the reactor that ran itself for a few hundred thousand years
scope: An anomaly-detection story with a two-billion-year-old answer. T1: May 1972, at a French uranium-processing plant, a routine check found that ore from the Oklo mine in Gabon was SHORT of uranium-235 — 0.60 percent where every uranium sample ever measured, on Earth, on the Moon and in meteorites, gives about 0.72. Missing fissile uranium is a security matter, so investigators went looking for a thief. T2: there was no thief. The uranium had already been burned — roughly 1.7 billion years ago, in sixteen separate zones, groundwater soaking through unusually rich ore had acted as a neutron moderator and the deposit had gone critical entirely on its own, with nobody there. T3: why it cannot happen again — uranium-235 decays faster than uranium-238, so 1.7 billion years ago natural uranium was about 3.1 percent U-235, which is roughly what a modern power station is fuelled with. The Earth has simply run out of the right fuel. T4: it regulated itself, which is the best part — the reaction heated the groundwater until it boiled away; with the moderator gone the reaction stopped; a couple of hours later the water seeped back and it restarted. Roughly thirty minutes on, two and a half hours off, over and over, for a few hundred thousand years, never much above 100 kilowatts. T5: how anyone can possibly know all that — the fission products are still sitting in the rock with impossible isotope ratios. Oklo neodymium is under 6 percent neodymium-142 where ordinary neodymium is 27 percent; its ruthenium is 27-30 percent ruthenium-99 where nature gives 12.7, exactly the leftovers of decaying technetium-99. Xenon isotopes trapped in the minerals even record the on-off cycle.
source: Wikipedia 'Natural nuclear fission reactor' (discovered May 1972 via mass spectrometry at the Tricastin enrichment facility, Pierrelatte; samples at 0.60% U-235 against the expected 0.72%, some ore as low as 0.44%; CEA announcement 25 September 1972; sixteen sites at Oklo; operation ~1.7 billion years ago for a few hundred thousand years, never much above 100 kW thermal; natural uranium about 3.1% U-235 at the time; groundwater moderator with a self-regulating cycle of about 30 minutes critical and 2.5 hours cooling; neodymium-142 under 6% versus 27% natural, ruthenium-99 at 27-30% versus 12.7% natural from technetium-99 decay; trapped xenon isotopes recording the cycle).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY ladder that is really a detective story, and the sub-strand's best demonstration that isotope ratios are EVIDENCE. T1 keys the ACT (a routine accounting check finds fissile material missing and someone goes looking for a thief) and inverts the wonder properly — the astonishing number, 0.60 against a universal 0.72, is in the stem, and the explanation is the answer. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) the CEA's 1972 announcement said 'about 2 billion years'; the refined figure is about 1.7 billion — pick 1.7 and do not present the two as a conflict. (2) The 30-minutes-on / 2.5-hours-off cycle is inferred from trapped xenon, not observed; a rung stating it must be paired with T5's evidence or it becomes an unsupported claim. (3) Oklo was never a bomb and never a runaway — power stayed at or below about 100 kW, which is a domestic space heater's worth per zone, and the ladder must not let 'natural nuclear reactor' become 'natural nuclear explosion'. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (it turned itself off when it got too hot and back on when it cooled, for hundreds of thousands of years). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real explanations investigators actually had to rule out — theft or diversion, laboratory contamination, an instrument fault, an exotic ore chemistry — plus real adjacent nuclear facts (enrichment, moderators, control rods, critical mass, Chicago Pile-1).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY bank owns place-tours of Gabon and of mining districts. This ladder never tours Oklo as a place: every rung keys to the isotope anomaly and the nuclear physics, and Gabon appears only as the address of the ore.

name: Moseley's X-rays — what an element's number really counts
scope: MINI gem: the measurement that gave the periodic table a physical spine, and the man it cost. T1: 1913-14, Henry Moseley fires electrons at one metal target after another and measures the X-ray wavelength each one gives back. The frequencies fall on a clean staircase, one step per element, with no room anywhere to squeeze an extra element in between — so the elements are not merely ordered, they are COUNTED, and what is being counted is the positive charge in the nucleus. T2: the fixes it forced — chemists had been ordering the table by atomic weight and quietly papering over the places where that misbehaved. Moseley's staircase puts cobalt before nickel even though nickel is the lighter, and tellurium before iodine for the same reason; Mendeleev had swapped both pairs on chemical instinct, and Moseley showed why his instinct was right. T3: the staircase also had four empty steps, at 43, 61, 72 and 75 — technetium, promethium, hafnium and rhenium, all found later — and it settled that there are exactly fifteen rare earths, ending decades of false element claims. He volunteered for the army and was shot dead as a signals officer at Gallipoli on 10 August 1915, aged 27, with the Nobel he would almost certainly have won still unawarded; Isaac Asimov called his death arguably the most costly single death of the war to mankind.
source: Wikipedia 'Henry Moseley' (X-ray spectra measured by crystal diffraction, 1913, Manchester then Oxford from November 1913; the systematic relation between X-ray wavelength and atomic number; the table reordered by nuclear charge rather than atomic weight, with cobalt and nickel as the classic case; gaps predicted at 43, 61, 72 and 75, later technetium, promethium, hafnium and rhenium; exactly fifteen lanthanides confirmed; killed at Gallipoli 10 August 1915 aged 27; Asimov's assessment of the loss).
framing_note: A mini ladder because its wonder is concentrated: the elements have a NUMBER, and the number is a count of charges in the nucleus, not a weight. No T1 rung — the concept needs a little scaffolding, so this starts at T2. ACCURACY RAIL: Moseley did not invent the idea of atomic number (van den Broek had proposed that the ordinal number equals the nuclear charge in 1911); Moseley MEASURED it and made it undeniable. Any rung crediting him with the idea is wrong; credit him with the evidence. Second rail: the Asimov line is a real published assessment and must be attributed to Asimov as an opinion, not stated as fact. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (chemists had the order right by instinct and nobody could say why until a young man with an X-ray tube counted the charges). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent people (Mendeleev, van den Broek, Bohr, Rutherford, Bragg) and the real wrong ordering principle, atomic weight, plus the genuinely disputed element claims of the period. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'atomic number is nuclear charge' before asking what the X-ray staircase revealed.
history_overlap: CHEMISTRY section (same bank) owns Mendeleev and the building of the periodic table. This ladder owns only the X-RAY MEASUREMENT that put a physical number under it — if a chemistry ladder already keys the cobalt/nickel and tellurium/iodine reversals to Mendeleev's chemical instinct, key them here to Moseley's spectrometer instead. HISTORY owns the Gallipoli campaign; the science rung is the loss of the measurer, not the battle.

name: Szilard's traffic light — the chain reaction nobody wanted
scope: A REVERSAL in which the greatest living authority and an unemployed refugee disagreed on the same day, and the refugee was right. T1: 11 September 1933 — Ernest Rutherford, the man who had discovered the nucleus, told the British Association at Leicester that anyone expecting a source of power from the transformation of atoms was talking moonshine. T2: the next morning in London, Leo Szilard read the report in The Times, went out walking, and while waiting for a light to change on Southampton Row realised that if some element could be made to spit out TWO neutrons for every one it swallowed, the thing would feed itself: a self-sustaining chain, and effectively unlimited energy. Twenty-four hours after the world's leading nuclear physicist said it was impossible. T3: what he did next is the strange part — Szilard patented the chain reaction in 1934 and assigned the patent to the British Admiralty specifically so it would be kept secret. A scientist trying to bury his own idea. T4: the idea then sat idle for five years, because Szilard had no candidate: no one knew of any nucleus that would actually do it. That gap closed only when Hahn, Strassmann, Meitner and Frisch showed in 1939 that uranium splits AND throws off spare neutrons when it does. T5: the physics made visible — Chicago, 2 December 1942, a stack of graphite blocks and uranium under the stands at Stagg Field, with cadmium rods pulled out inch by inch until the neutron count stopped falling and started climbing on its own. That is what 'critical' means: below a certain mass the neutrons escape faster than they multiply, and above it they do not.
source: Wikipedia 'Leo Szilard' (Rutherford's September 1933 remark that anyone looking for a source of power in the transformation of atoms was 'talking moonshine'; Szilard reading the report in The Times on the morning of 12 September 1933; the chain-reaction insight at a traffic light on Southampton Row, Bloomsbury, that same day; the patent filed June 1934, granted March 1936, assigned to the British Admiralty under the Patents and Designs Act to keep it secret). Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission' (Szilard's 1933 conception following Rutherford's dismissal; Chicago Pile-1 first criticality, 2 December 1942, under Fermi). Grokipedia 'Ernest Rutherford' consulted for the 1919 transmutation and nuclear-model context.
framing_note: A REVERSAL ladder about authority. Starts at T2 because the concept needs the neutron already established. VOICE: active, named, no agent-hiding — Rutherford said it, Szilard read it, Szilard filed it. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) the traffic-light moment rests on Szilard's own later recollection, so tell it as his account, not as an observed event; Richard Rhodes's 'The Making of the Atomic Bomb' is the standard secondary source and the build should cite it rather than assert the scene flatly. (2) Rutherford's 'moonshine' judgement was reasonable given 1933 physics — accelerators then consumed far more energy than any transmutation returned — and the rung must present it as a defensible expert call that a new fact overturned, not as stupidity. That is the whole lesson: consensus is not evidence, and being right once does not make you right next time. (3) Do not let a rung imply Szilard predicted fission; he predicted the chain-reaction PRINCIPLE and had no idea which nucleus would supply it, which is exactly what T4 is for. Dinner-test payoff: T1 plus T2 told together — the discoverer of the nucleus said no, and a man at a crosswalk said yes, one day apart. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent people (Rutherford, Fermi, Meitner, Frisch, Hahn, Joliot-Curie, Chadwick) and the real wrong candidates of the mid-1930s (beryllium, indium and other elements Szilard actually tested and ruled out). GRADE-10 CEILING: criticality is presented as neutron bookkeeping — do they multiply faster than they leak out — with no reactor kinetics.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank owns the Manhattan Project, the Einstein-Szilard letter and the Second World War. Every rung here keys to the PHYSICS of neutron multiplication and criticality and to the Rutherford/Szilard reversal; bomb targets, wartime politics and the 1939 letter stay out entirely, and Chicago Pile-1 appears only as the demonstration of criticality.
